title: Container Adaptors
relevance: Interviewers probe stack/queue/priority_queue defaults, why adaptors hide iterators, and how to build min-heaps and custom comparators for BFS/DFS/Dijkstra-style code.

phases.goal: Establish that adaptors wrap a sequence container and publish only a narrow LIFO, FIFO, or priority API with no iterators.

must_hit.point: A container adaptor is not a new container; it wraps an underlying sequence container and restricts the interface to specialised behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says it wraps deque/vector/list (etc.) and exposes only the adaptor’s narrow API, not a general sequence.

must_hit.point: The three standard adaptors are std::stack, std::queue, and std::priority_queue.
Adaptors intentionally expose no iterators: no traversal, no range-based for, and no indexed access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States you cannot iterate or index; only manipulate via the adaptor’s strict operations.

must_hit.point: All three are thin wrappers that forward to the underlying container (and for priority_queue, to heap algorithms in <algorithm>).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions forwarding and that choosing the underlying container changes performance, not the public API.

probes: What is a container adaptor in C++, and how does it differ from a normal sequence container?
Why do stack, queue, and priority_queue have no iterators?

hints.2: Name the three adaptors and what each access pattern allows.
hints.3: Adaptor = underlying container + narrow LIFO/FIFO/priority API; no begin/end or indexing.

phases.goal: Cover defaults, required underlying ops, interfaces, heap layout, and comparator/min-heap rules.

must_hit.point: std::stack defaults to std::deque<T>; the underlying container must support push_back, pop_back, and back (vector or list also work).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the template default as deque and lists the three required operations.

must_hit.point: std::queue defaults to std::deque<T> and needs push_back, pop_front, front, and back; std::vector is not valid because it lacks efficient pop_front.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says deque default, list OK, vector ill-formed/useless for lacking pop_front.

must_hit.point: std::priority_queue defaults to std::vector<T> and Compare = std::less, yielding a max-heap; it is a binary heap over a random-access container.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States vector default, less → max-heap, binary-heap implementation.

must_hit.point: For a binary heap in a vector (0-based), left child is at 2*i+1, right at 2*i+2, parent at (i-1)/2; top is c.front() at index 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the index formulas and that top is the root at index 0.

must_hit.point: priority_queue push/emplace/pop are O(log n); top is O(1); stack/queue push and pop are amortised O(1) with O(1) top/front/back/size/empty.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Matches the complexity table: heap logarithmic push/pop, constant top; stack/queue amortised O(1) ends.

must_hit.point: pop() returns void on all three; read with top()/front() first. priority_queue::top returns const T& only so the heap invariant cannot be broken by mutation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says void pop, read-then-pop pattern, and const-only top on priority_queue.

must_hit.point: A min-heap needs Compare = std::greater and thus an explicit Container (usually std::vector<T>); comparator returns true when the first argument has lower priority than the second.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<T>> and explains the lower-priority / inverted comparator rule.

must_hit.point: priority_queue has no decrease-key or iteration; contest workaround is push duplicates and lazy-skip stale entries when top distance is worse than best known.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes push-new-pair + skip-if-stale (Dijkstra-style), not in-place key updates.

probes: What are the default underlying containers for stack, queue, and priority_queue, and why can’t queue use vector?
How do you make a min-heap with std::priority_queue, and how is the heap stored in the vector?
Why does priority_queue::top return const T&, and what does pop return?

hints.1: Defaults differ: ends vs random access.
hints.2: Queue needs both ends; priority_queue needs heap ops on a random-access sequence plus Compare.
hints.3: deque for stack/queue, vector + less (max-heap) for priority_queue; min-heap = greater; children 2i+1/2i+2; void pop; const top.

phases.goal: Judge when to pick each adaptor and which underlying container fits growth, ends, and random-access needs.

must_hit.point: deque is stack’s default because it grows efficiently at both ends without vector’s occasional large reallocations, while still giving amortised O(1) push_back/pop_back/back; prefer vector when the stack stays small or cache locality matters more.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts deque growth vs vector reallocations and when vector is preferable.

must_hit.point: Queue needs efficient ops at both ends, so deque or list; stack only needs the back end. priority_queue needs random access (vector or deque), not list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties FIFO both-ends requirement to deque/list and heap random-access to vector/deque.

must_hit.point: Use stack/queue when the algorithm’s discipline is the point (DFS/BFS); use priority_queue when you always need the current best key; if you need decrease-key, arbitrary deletes, or sorted iteration, use set/multiset or another heap instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps adaptors to DFS/BFS vs Dijkstra/top-K and names set when the adaptor API is too narrow.

probes: When would you back a stack with vector instead of the default deque?
When is priority_queue the wrong tool compared to set?

hints.1: Match ends and access pattern to the container.
hints.2: Stack = back only; queue = front+back; heap = random access + top only.
hints.3: deque default for stack/queue; vector for priority_queue; set when you need decrease-key or ordered walk.

phases.goal: Apply adaptors to classic interview patterns and correct comparator/custom-type setup.

must_hit.point: Classic stack uses: matching brackets, explicit-stack DFS, undo/redo, postfix evaluation; no iterators because the contract is LIFO-only.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists those uses and ties missing iterators to preserving LIFO abstraction.

must_hit.point: Queues power BFS, sliding-window problems, and producer–consumer buffering.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names BFS / sliding window / producer–consumer as queue roles.

must_hit.point: For custom types, supply a functor with operator() or a lambda with decltype(cmp) and pass cmp to the constructor; stateful lambdas fail if default-constructed without pq(cmp).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows functor or decltype(cmp) + constructor argument; warns about capturing lambdas without passing cmp.

must_hit.point: Python list simulates stack, collections.deque a queue, and heapq a min-heap by default—unlike C++ priority_queue’s max-heap default.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts Python heapq min-heap default with C++ max-heap default.

probes: Give interview uses of stack vs queue vs priority_queue.
How do you put a custom struct into a priority_queue with a lambda comparator?

hints.1: Map LIFO / FIFO / best-key to algorithms.
hints.2: Think brackets/DFS vs BFS vs Dijkstra/top-K, plus comparator wiring.
hints.3: Stack: brackets/DFS; queue: BFS; priority_queue: best key; lambda needs decltype(cmp) and pq(cmp).

tradeoffs.topic: deque vs vector as stack backing
tradeoffs.strong_answer: deque is default: efficient growth at ends without vector’s occasional large reallocations, still amortised O(1) back ops; choose vector when the stack stays small or cache locality matters more than growth behaviour.

tradeoffs.topic: deque/list vs vector as queue backing
tradeoffs.strong_answer: queue needs efficient push_back and pop_front plus front/back, so deque (default) or list work; vector is invalid/poor because it lacks efficient pop_front.

tradeoffs.topic: vector/deque vs list as priority_queue backing
tradeoffs.strong_answer: priority_queue needs random access for heap algorithms, so vector (default) or deque; list lacks random access and is not a fit.

priority_queue when you only need push/pop/top of the current best key; if you need decrease-key, arbitrary deletes, or sorted iteration, use set/multiset (or a hand-rolled/policy-based heap) instead.

tradeoffs.topic: C++ priority_queue max-heap vs Python heapq min-heap
tradeoffs.strong_answer: C++ default Compare is std::less → max-heap; Python heapq defaults to a min-heap—so the same ‘default PQ’ mental model does not transfer.

gotchas.trap: Calling pop() and expecting the removed value.
gotchas.correction: pop() returns void on stack, queue, and priority_queue; always read with top()/front() first, then pop().

gotchas.trap: Calling top/front/back/pop on an empty adaptor.
gotchas.correction: Those operations on an empty stack or queue are undefined behaviour; check empty() first.

gotchas.trap: Mutating the element returned by priority_queue::top().
gotchas.correction: top() returns const T& only; mutating through the adaptor would break the heap invariant.

gotchas.trap: Writing a comparator as return a.priority > b.priority expecting a max-heap of priority.
gotchas.correction: Return true when a has lower priority than b; std::less yields a max-heap, std::greater a min-heap—the intuition feels inverted.

gotchas.trap: Declaring priority_queue<T, vector<T>, decltype(cmp)> pq; without pq(cmp) for a capturing lambda.
gotchas.correction: Pass the lambda to the constructor; default-constructing the comparator only works for a stateless lambda.

gotchas.trap: Using std::vector as the underlying container for std::queue.
gotchas.correction: vector has no efficient pop_front; use deque (default) or list.

gotchas.trap: Expecting to iterate a priority_queue in priority order or decrease a key in place.
gotchas.correction: No iterators and no decrease-key; walk by destructive top+pop, or use push-duplicates with lazy deletion / switch to set.
